```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.2, out.width = "100%", dpi = 110)
options(digits = 4)
```

mediamix turns raw marketing data into model-ready features. It does two
things, and deliberately not a third: it converts media spend into
carryover- and saturation-adjusted regressors, and it converts raw event logs
into attributed customer journeys. It does not fit models. `lm()`, `glmnet`
and `brms` already do that better than a marketing package would.

This vignette walks the whole arc on the media side: raw weekly spend, through
diagnostics and transforms, to a fitted model, contributions and return on
investment. It uses `mm_weekly`, three years of synthetic weekly spend, price
and revenue for three geographies, generated from known parameters so that
the estimates can be checked against the truth. Most of the work is on the
north geography:

```{r}
library(mediamix)
data(mm_weekly)

north <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$geo == "north", ]
channels <- c("tv", "video", "search", "social", "display")
str(north[, c("date", channels, "price", "revenue")])
```

## Look before you transform

Many marketing mix projects fail for reasons visible in the data before any
model is fitted. `diagnose_media()` checks for five of them: channels that move
together, channels that barely vary, channels that are dark (spend nothing) in
most weeks, an erratic cost per mille when impressions are supplied, and,
given a `date` column, rows out of time order, repeated weeks and gaps, none
of which adstock notices, since it takes adjacent rows as adjacent weeks. With
`by = "geo"` it runs each check within each geography and reports the worst
case.

```{r}
diagnose_media(mm_weekly, media = channels, by = "geo", date = "date")
```

Nothing structural is wrong here, which is what you would expect from
synthetic data. On real data this is where you learn that two channels were
planned together and their coefficients will therefore flip sign on small
changes to the specification. The detail is in the elements the printout
names, starting with the spend statistics in `$variation`:

```{r}
d <- diagnose_media(mm_weekly, media = channels, by = "geo")
d$variation
```

With `by` supplied, `cv`, `distinct` and `zero_share` report the worst case
across series, which is what you want from a diagnostic, while `mean` and `sd`
are averages over the series. So read `zero_share`, the share of weeks with no
spend, as the worst geography's rate, not an overall average. `video` goes dark
in `r round(100 * d$variation$zero_share[d$variation$channel == "video"])`% of
weeks in its worst geography and `display` in
`r round(100 * d$variation$zero_share[d$variation$channel == "display"])`%.
That is normal, because media is flighted (bought in bursts with gaps between
them), but it means those channels carry less information than
`r nrow(north)` weeks per geography suggests.

## Carryover

Advertising does not stop working the week it runs. Adstock spreads each
period's spend forward with geometric decay, using a set of weights called the
kernel.

```{r}
spend <- c(100, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)
round(adstock_geometric(spend, decay = 0.5), 2)
```

By default the kernel's weights sum to one, so the burst of 100 is spread out
rather than repeated: half of it lands in the week of spend, a quarter in the
week after, and so on. The section on normalisation below says why that
matters.

Practitioners think in half-lives, not decay coefficients, so the package
provides the translation:

```{r}
theta <- decay_from_half_life(3)   # a three-week half-life on weekly data
theta
half_life(theta)
effective_window(theta, coverage = 0.90)
```

`decay_from_half_life(3)` is the weekly decay for a three-week half-life, and
`half_life()` converts it back. The last line says that carryover with this
half-life needs `r effective_window(theta, coverage = 0.90)` weeks to deliver
90% of its effect, which is how you decide whether truncating the kernel (the
`max_lag` argument) costs you anything, and whether `r nrow(north)` weeks of
data can identify a carryover this long at all.

### Normalisation changes what your coefficient means

`normalise` is the argument that most often changes an answer without anyone
noticing, so it is explicit rather than implied.

```{r}
constant <- rep(100, 50)
tail(adstock_geometric(constant, decay = 0.8), 1)
tail(adstock_geometric(constant, decay = 0.8, normalise = FALSE), 1)
```

Normalised, the kernel sums to 1: once the filter has filled up, a constant
spend of 100 adstocks to 100, the series level is preserved, and the fitted
coefficient reads as the effect of *one unit of media*. Unnormalised (raw Koyck
accumulation), the same series accumulates to `100 / (1 - 0.8)`, and the
coefficient reads as the effect of one unit of *accumulated* media. Both are
defensible. Comparing a coefficient fitted one way against a coefficient
fitted the other is not.

mediamix defaults to normalised, as does the Bayesian media mix model of Jin
et al. (2017). Robyn's geometric adstock does not, so if you are reconciling
against Robyn, set `normalise = FALSE`.

### Dark weeks

Media data is full of zero-spend weeks, and carryover has to survive them:

```{r}
flighted <- c(100, 100, 0, 0, 0, 0, 100)
round(adstock_geometric(flighted, decay = 0.6), 2)
```

Carryover decays across the gap rather than resetting, and the new burst adds
to what is left.

### Delayed peaks

A geometric kernel always peaks in the period of spend. Television and
out-of-home often do not, and no decay rate fixes that. Weibull adstock with
`type = "pdf"` can, and so can the delayed kernel of Jin et al. (2017), whose
`peak` is read directly in weeks. The three kernels' weights over eight weeks:

```{r}
w_geo <- adstock_weights(8, decay = 0.6)
w_wei <- adstock_weights_weibull(8, shape = 2, scale = 3, type = "pdf")
w_del <- adstock_weights_delayed(8, decay = 0.6, peak = 2)
round(rbind(geometric = w_geo, weibull = w_wei, delayed = w_del), 3)
which.max(w_wei)
```

The first column is the week of spend. The Weibull kernel's largest weight is
in column `r which.max(w_wei)`, `r which.max(w_wei) - 1` week after the spend,
and the delayed kernel's is `r which.max(w_del) - 1` weeks after it. The three
shapes side by side:

```{r kernels, fig.height = 3.6}
cols <- mm_palette(3)
ink <- mm_palette(role = "ink")
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1), bg = ink[["surface"]], fg = ink[["axis"]])
matplot(0:7, cbind(w_geo, w_wei, w_del), type = "o", pch = 19, lty = 1,
        lwd = 2, col = cols, xlab = "Weeks after spend",
        ylab = "Share of the effect", las = 1, bty = "n",
        col.axis = ink[["muted"]], col.lab = ink[["secondary"]])
legend("topright", c("geometric, decay 0.6", "Weibull pdf, shape 2",
                     "delayed, peak at week 2"),
       col = cols, lwd = 2, pch = 19, bty = "n", text.col = ink[["secondary"]])
par(op)
```

## Saturation

Adstock says *when* money works. Saturation says how hard it works at the
margin. `saturate_hill()` maps media onto a share of the channel's ceiling,
between 0 and 1. Its `half_max` is the spend at which the response reaches half
its ceiling, which is interpretable in the units you actually budget in. Its
`shape` sets the form of the curve: `shape = 1`, the default, is concave, and
`shape > 1` produces the threshold effect below which media barely registers.
Both forms at six levels of spend, with `half_max` at 100,000:

```{r}
levels <- c(0, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400) * 1000
round(rbind(
  concave = saturate_hill(levels, half_max = 100000),
  s_shape = saturate_hill(levels, half_max = 100000, shape = 3)
), 3)
```

```{r saturation, fig.height = 3.6}
grid_spend <- seq(0, 400000, by = 2000)
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1), bg = ink[["surface"]], fg = ink[["axis"]])
plot(grid_spend / 1000, saturate_hill(grid_spend, half_max = 100000),
     type = "l", lwd = 2, col = cols[1], ylim = c(0, 1), las = 1, bty = "n",
     xlab = "Spend (thousands)", ylab = "Share of the ceiling",
     col.axis = ink[["muted"]], col.lab = ink[["secondary"]])
lines(grid_spend / 1000, saturate_hill(grid_spend, 100000, shape = 3),
      lwd = 2, col = cols[2])
abline(v = 100, col = ink[["muted"]])
text(100, 0.05, "half_max", pos = 4, cex = 0.8, col = ink[["muted"]])
legend("bottomright", c("shape = 1, concave", "shape = 3, S-shaped"),
       col = cols[1:2], lwd = 2, bty = "n", text.col = ink[["secondary"]])
par(op)
```

Both curves reach half the ceiling at `half_max`. Below it the S-shaped curve
barely registers; above it, the S-shaped curve closes on the ceiling faster
than the concave one.

## Composing carryover and saturation in the right order

Saturation goes *after* adstock. Saturating first puts each period's spend
through the curve in isolation, so carryover from earlier periods never counts
towards saturation; with `normalise = FALSE` the kernel weights sum to more
than one and carryover also lifts the result past the ceiling.
`media_transform()` composes them in the right order and warns if asked to
reverse it.

`mm_weekly` was generated from known parameters, attached as its `"truth"`
attribute, so here we can transform each channel with the right decay,
`half_max` and `shape`. A `saturation` list without a `type` uses the Hill
curve. On real data you do not know these parameters: `vignette("carryover")`
shows how to choose the decays, and `vignette("tidymodels")` how to tune them
together with the saturation parameters.

`spec` holds one entry per channel, in the form `media_transform()` takes, and
`transform_plan()` runs each channel's column of the plan through its own
entry:

```{r}
truth <- attr(mm_weekly, "truth")

spec <- lapply(stats::setNames(channels, channels), function(ch) list(
  adstock = list(decay = truth$decay[[ch]]),
  saturation = list(half_max = truth$half_max[[ch]],
                    shape = truth$shape[[ch]])
))
transformed <- transform_plan(north, spec)[channels]
round(head(transformed, 4), 4)
```

Each column is now a share of its channel's ceiling, between 0 and 1.

## Fit whatever model you like

mediamix stops here. The transformed columns are ordinary numeric vectors, so
any modelling function will take them. Here `lm()` fits revenue on the five
channels and the controls the data were simulated with (a weekly trend, price,
the seasonal index and a December flag). The output sets the estimates against
the true coefficients, then gives each estimate's error in per cent:

```{r}
model_data <- transformed
model_data$week <- seq_len(nrow(model_data))
model_data$price <- north$price
model_data$seasonality <- north$seasonality
model_data$holiday <- north$holiday

fit <- lm(north$revenue ~ ., data = model_data)
estimates <- rbind(estimate = coef(fit)[channels],
                   truth = truth$beta[channels])
round(estimates)
round(100 * (estimates["estimate", ] / estimates["truth", ] - 1))
```

Close, not exact: the estimates miss the truth by between
`r min(abs(round(100 * (estimates["estimate", ] / estimates["truth", ] - 1))))`%
and `r max(abs(round(100 * (estimates["estimate", ] / estimates["truth", ] - 1))))`%.
`r nrow(north)` weekly observations of flighted, mildly correlated media is a
hard estimation problem, and pretending otherwise is how marketing mix models
acquire their reputation.

The controls are doing real work. Drop them and the media coefficients absorb
the trend and the price effect instead:

```{r}
bare <- lm(north$revenue ~ ., data = transformed)
round(rbind(true = truth$beta[channels],
            with_controls = coef(fit)[channels],
            without = coef(bare)[channels]))
```

Without them `r sum(coef(bare)[channels] < 0)` of the
`r length(channels)` media coefficients turn negative, and `search` collapses from `r round(coef(fit)[["search"]])` to
`r round(coef(bare)[["search"]])`. Nothing about the transform changed; the
specification did.

## Contributions and ROI

A marketing mix deliverable is the decomposition rather than the
coefficients: how much of predicted revenue each channel produced.
`contributions()` multiplies each transformed channel by its coefficient, week
by week, and pools everything else the model predicts into a `"(baseline)"`
channel. Totals over the three years:

```{r}
contrib <- contributions(transformed, fit, index = north$date)
round(tapply(contrib$contribution, contrib$channel, sum))
```

`"(baseline)"` is everything the model predicts that this decomposition does
not attribute to the supplied media: the intercept, the trend, price,
seasonality and the December uplift, pooled. It is *not* organic demand, and
reporting it as such is a common way for one of these decks to overstate its
own precision.

Pooling the rest into the baseline is what makes the arithmetic close exactly:
in every week, the contributions sum to the model's fitted value.

```{r}
totals <- as.numeric(tapply(contrib$contribution, contrib$period, sum))
all.equal(totals, unname(fitted(fit)))
```

Media's share of predicted revenue over the three years:

```{r}
media_share <- 1 - sum(contrib$contribution[contrib$channel == "(baseline)"]) /
  sum(contrib$contribution)
round(media_share, 3)
```

Media accounts for `r round(100 * media_share)`% of predicted revenue here,
and the baseline for the rest. Over time, with the baseline left out so the
media is visible:

```{r contributions-plot}
plot(contrib)
```

The dip at the very start of 2023 is the cold start: television's long
carryover takes weeks to fill from zero. `adstock_steady_state()` removes it
when that matters, as `vignette("carryover")` shows.

`roi()` divides each channel's total contribution by its total spend, which
gives the average return per pound, and sorts the channels by it:

```{r}
roi(contrib, north[channels])
```

### Average and marginal return are different questions

Average ROI is a scorecard. Marginal ROI, what the *next* pound returns, is the
decision variable, and it is the only one of the two that should drive a
reallocation.

The tempting shortcut is to differentiate the saturation curve at the mean
adstocked level and multiply by the kernel's first weight, `1 - decay`, on the
grounds that a pound spent this week only adds that much to this week's
adstock. It does, but it also adds to every later week's adstock, and under a
normalised kernel those contributions sum to the whole pound. The shortcut
measures the return *inside the week of spend* and ignores the rest, which for
a slow channel is most of it.

`marginal_roi()` avoids the calculus altogether. It re-runs the full transform
on a budget 1% larger in every week and divides the extra response by the
extra spend, the definition used by Jin et al. (2017) and by Google's
Meridian, so carryover and flighting are both handled by construction, and the
result is a total over the same weeks as the average. Given the spend plan,
the coefficients and `spec`, it does every channel at once:

```{r}
marginal <- marginal_roi(north, coef(fit), spec = spec)
marginal[, c("channel", "roi", "mroi")]
```

Because both are totals over the observed weeks, response that the last weeks'
spend would produce after the data end is not counted. For a budget decision,
the `extend` argument counts it; `?marginal_roi` shows how much it matters.

Compare the shortcut for television, whose decay of
`r truth$decay[["tv"]]` means only `r 100 * (1 - truth$decay[["tv"]])`% of a
week's spend lands in that week's adstock:

```{r}
z_tv <- adstock_geometric(north$tv, decay = truth$decay[["tv"]])
shortcut <- mroi(mean(z_tv), coefficient = coef(fit)[["tv"]],
                 half_max = truth$half_max[["tv"]],
                 shape = truth$shape[["tv"]]) * (1 - truth$decay[["tv"]])
c(shortcut = shortcut, simulated = marginal$mroi[marginal$channel == "tv"])
```

The shortcut understates television's marginal return about
`r round(marginal$mroi[marginal$channel == "tv"] / shortcut)`-fold, and a
reallocation built on it would strip budget from exactly the channel whose
effect arrives late.

Read the `mroi` column of the `marginal_roi()` table instead. In this fitted
model display's average pound returns about
`r round(marginal$roi[marginal$channel == "display"], 1)`, but its *next* pound
returns `r round(marginal$mroi[marginal$channel == "display"], 2)`, less than it
costs, and the average-ROI table hides that completely. Search and social have
average returns
`r round(with(marginal, roi / mroi)[marginal$channel == "search"], 1)` and
`r round(with(marginal, roi / mroi)[marginal$channel == "social"], 1)` times
their marginal ones: concave curves, well up the slope. Television is the odd
one out: its marginal return is close to its average, because its S-shaped
curve (a `shape` of `r truth$shape[["tv"]]`) is still near its steepest
section at this budget. Under a concave curve marginal is below average everywhere;
under an S-curve it can be close to or even above it below the inflection
point, and assuming otherwise is how a threshold channel stays starved.

Every figure above comes from a model fitted to `r nrow(north)` noisy weeks.
The data were simulated, so the fitted marginal returns can be set against the
ones the true coefficients give:

```{r}
true_marginal <- marginal_roi(north, truth$beta, spec = spec)
true_mroi <- stats::setNames(true_marginal$mroi, true_marginal$channel)
round(rbind(fitted = stats::setNames(marginal$mroi, marginal$channel),
            truth = true_mroi), 2)
```

With the true coefficients display's next pound returns
`r round(true_mroi[["display"]], 2)`, and the channels rank differently. Sampling
noise in three years of weekly data is enough to move a marginal return across
break-even, which is why a reallocation suggested by these numbers should be
tested before it is made. The
[budget walkthrough](https://elkronos.github.io/mediamix/articles/budget-walkthrough.html)
on the package website puts bootstrap intervals on these marginal returns with
`block_bootstrap()` and tests a reallocation before recommending one.

### The response curve

`response_curve()` evaluates one channel's fitted curve, its coefficient times
its saturation curve, at a range of adstocked media levels, and gives the
marginal return at each. Under a normalised kernel a steady weekly spend
settles at the same adstocked level, so the spend axis can be read as
sustained weekly spend. `spend_for()` inverts the curve: it returns the level
that reaches a target response. For television:

```{r response-curve, fig.height = 5.5}
curve <- response_curve(
  spend = seq(0, 6000, by = 1000),
  coefficient = coef(fit)[["tv"]],
  half_max = truth$half_max[["tv"]], shape = truth$shape[["tv"]]
)
curve

fine <- response_curve(seq(0, 6000, by = 50), coefficient = coef(fit)[["tv"]],
                       half_max = truth$half_max[["tv"]],
                       shape = truth$shape[["tv"]])
plot(fine, observed = adstock_geometric(north$tv, truth$decay[["tv"]]))

level <- spend_for(target = 3000, coefficient = coef(fit)[["tv"]],
                   half_max = truth$half_max[["tv"]],
                   shape = truth$shape[["tv"]])
level
```

The marginal return peaks at a level of
`r fine$spend[which.max(fine$marginal)]`, where the S-shaped curve is
steepest. The plot shades everything above
`r round(max(adstock_geometric(north$tv, truth$decay[["tv"]])))`, the highest
adstocked level in the data, as extrapolation. `spend_for()` puts a weekly
response of 3000 at a level of `r round(level)`, near the top of the observed
range.

These describe the curve the model fitted, which is not the same as what would
happen if you actually spent that much. The curve is identified only over the
range of spend the data contains; anything beyond it is extrapolation wearing
a decimal point.
